State the problem or question (e.g., describe the population, disease, current standard of care, if one exists, and limitations of knowledge or available therapy) and the reason for conducting the clinical trial <Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a chronic liver disease resulting from excessive fat accumulation in the liver which may be accompanied by inflammation (steatohepatitis) and fibrosis. This in turn can progress to cirrhosis and end-stage liver disease. NAFLD is considered the hepatic manifestation of metabolic syndrome, which is characterized by insulin resistance, visceral obesity, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and abnormalities of fasting serum glucose levels. Due to its close association with obesity, it has become the most common liver disease in children and adolescents in the United States. Furthermore, it has become one of the leading indications for liver transplantation in adults [1]. The prevalence of both NAFLD and obesity is increasing due to sedentary lifestyles and hypercaloric diets [2]. According to epidemiological data, NAFLD may affect 3–10 % of pediatric patients, with a male- to-female ratio of 2:1 [2]. The prevalence varies by method of detection, which may include screening by alanine aminotransferase (ALT), imaging for steatosis, or confirmation by liver biopsy. In North America, NAFLD prevalence ranges from 0.7% in young children ages 2 to 4 years (confirmed at autopsy), to 29% to 38% in obese children (by studies of ALT elevation). Several studies have suggested that gut-liver axis malfunction [small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), intestinal dysbiosis, and increased intestinal permeability (“leaky gut”)] is the leading factor in the development and progression of NAFLD [3]. The currently recommended screening test, ALT, is an inexpensive, universally available blood test. ALT is minimally invasive and has an acceptable sensitivity but poor specificity. Imaging has also been used as a screening tool for NAFLD. <Protocol Title> Version <x.x>

Clinically available, routine ultrasonography performs poorly for the detection of steatosis in children because of its low sensitivity and specificity particularly in children who have lower degrees of steatosis (ie, involving <33% of hepatocytes) or in individuals with BMI ≥40 [4]. In addition, routine ultrasound is not able to quantify steatosis or fibrosis in children with NAFLD. A more precise ultrasound methodology has been developed in recent years under the name Fibroscan. Fibroscan is a non-invasive ultrasound-based method that uses shear wave velocity to assess tissue stiffness via transient elastography (TE) and uses radiofrequency ultrasound signals to assess steatosis via controlled attenuation parameter (CAP) [5]. However, it is not widely available. The limitations of ALT and ultrasonography as screening tools for NAFLD can lead to inconsistencies, as patients with NAFLD can have an ALT <40 U/L in the context of ultrasonography that suggests the presence of steatosis and vice versa [6]. The goal of this study is to evaluate the role of probiotics in the treatment of pediatric NAFLD by evaluating for steatosis and fibrosis with a Fibroscan machine. This will be done by performing a fibroscan during each visit and comparing patients’ ALT at various intervals. This is an important study as current pediatric guidelines only recommend lifestyle modifications for the treatment of NAFLD and the use of ALT and sonogram to assess improvement. We hypothesized that treatment with a probiotic will demonstrate an improvement in NAFLD as assessed by a fibroscan of liver which is good for the monitoring of steatosis and fibrosis. Additionally, analysis of fecal microbiome results may offer insight into targeted therapy in the future>

< NAFLD was first described in the pediatric population nearly 3 decades ago and has since emerged as the most common cause of liver disease in the developed world. NAFLD is a multifactorial disorder with a complex interplay between genetic, epigenetic, and environmental factors. It often coexists with components of metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes. The spectrum of NAFLD encompasses simple fat accumulation (NAFL) also often referred to as ‘simple steatosis’, steatohepatitis (NASH) with or without fibrosis, and cirrhosis [7]. Obesity is the best known clinical risk factor, and plays a significant role in the development of NAFLD. NAFLD has a male to female ratio of 2:1 and in children, the prevalence of NAFLD increases with age (<9 years: 3.3% and ≥15 years 17.3% in obese/overweight children). Despite its high prevalence and important health consequences, diagnosing and staging NAFLD in clinical practice remains complex as most patients are asymptomatic and no accurate screening tool exists. The currently recommended screening test is ALT which is an inexpensive, universally available blood test. ALT is minimally invasive <Protocol Title> Version <x.x>

Protocol <#> <DD Month YYYY>

and has an acceptable sensitivity but has poor specificity. US has also been used as a screening tool for NAFLD, but it also suffers from poor specificity and an inability to objectively quantify the degree of steatosis. Dysbiosis has been shown to contribute to the pathogenesis of NAFLD. Dysbiosis increases gut permeability to bacterial products and increases hepatic exposure to injurious substances that leads to hepatic inflammation and fibrosis [8]. The gastrointestinal tract harbors the largest number of bacteria, representing more than 150-fold their eukaryotic nuclear genome. This “microbial organ” is recognized to perform a variety of physiological functions, ranging from its protective purpose to metabolic regulation. This includes an active part in both glucose and lipid metabolism. Recent lines of evidence suggest a role of gut microbiota in insulin resistance and obesity. This information has raised an interest in gut microbiota as an active intervenient in NAFLD. There is a close anatomical and functional relationship between the gut and the liver, through portal circulation, favoring bidirectional influences [9]. Therefore, the gut microbiome may play an important role in the maintenance of gut-liver axis health. Dysbiosis combined with a poor diet appears to contribute to the pathogenesis of NAFLD [9]. The human gut microbiome is composed of a complex structure of trillions of organisms that contribute to the processing of different components of our diet such as carbohydrates, fats, and proteins. This microbiome serves as the gate that permits energy and caloric retention and subsequent development of obesity. Both genetics and environment play a role in obesity and its sequela, such as NAFLD. Studies on obese mice showed a 50% reduction in Bacteroidetes and an increase in Firmicutes by a comparable amount, demonstrating that ‘obesogenic microbiota’ is distinct from ‘lean microbiota’ [10]. These differences in microbiota composition in mice can determine the response to a high-fat diet and whether those mice will develop hepatic steatosis [11], as well as how the disease will progress [12]. Comparable observations are noted in human studies. Microbiota of obese adults had fewer Bacteroidetes [13] and more Firmicutes phyla resulting in difference in Bacteroidetes-to-Firmicutes ratio between obese and non-obese subjects, and the pattern was reversed with weight loss [14]. Recent evidence suggests that targeting the gut-liver axis using probiotics may be an appropriate approach for treating NAFLD. Manipulation of intestinal flora with probiotics in experimental rodent animal model of NAFLD did indeed have a beneficial effect. In humans, a preliminary study investigating the outcome of probiotic VSL#3 (a mixture of 4 lactobacilli strains) [15] and Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG therapy on NAFLD [16] patient yielded some promising results. The goal of treatment in NAFLD patients is regression of NAFLD, defined as a decrease in steatosis, inflammation, and/or fibrosis. A second accepted goal is resolution of NASH. Due to poor compliance with lifestyle modification, some studies indicate that a combination of these interventions along with pharmacological interventions and dietary supplementation could have a more favorable effect [17]. Among a recommended series of therapeutic dietary supplements, probiotics may be the most promising agents because of their safety, tolerability, and efficacy [17].> 2.3 RISK/BENEFIT ASSESSMENT

Expected adverse reactions are AEs that are known to occur for the study intervention being studied and should be collected in a standard, systematic format using a grading scale based on functional assessment or magnitude of reaction. Identify the source of the reference safety information used to determine the expectedness of the AE (e.g., IB, approved labeling). Expectedness is assessed based on the awareness of AEs previously observed, not on the basis of what might be anticipated from the properties of the study intervention. An AE or suspected adverse reaction is considered "unexpected" if it is not listed in the IB, package insert, or device labeling or is not listed at the specificity or severity that has been observed; or, if an IB is not required or available, is not consistent with the risk information described in the protocol, as amended. DEFINITION OF SERIOUS ADVERSE EVENTS (SAE)

Provide the definition of an SAE being used for the clinical trial. The FDA definition of an SAE is used in this template since this template is for phase 2 or 3 IND and IDE studies. It is important to note that FDA regulations require reporting based on the definition included in 21 CFR 312.32 (a) for studies performed under an IND, regardless of the definition of SAE used in the protocol. Therefore, investigators should develop an appropriate definition for their study. This definition could include an unanticipated adverse device effect, but an SAE is broader than that definition. Important medical events that may not result in death, be life-threatening, or require hospitalization may be considered serious when, based upon appropriate medical judgment, they may jeopardize the participant and may require medical or surgical intervention to prevent one of the outcomes listed in this definition. subsections.title: General Approach
subsections.content:
GENERAL APPROACH

As a guide, the following should be addressed, as appropriate:

 For descriptive statistics, describe how categorical and continuous data will be presented (e.g., percentages, means with standard deviations, median, range).

 For inferential tests, indicate the p-value and confidence intervals for statistical significance (Type I error) and whether one or two-tailed.

 Indicate whether covariates will be pre-specified in the sections below or later in a SAP.

 State whether checks of assumptions (e.g., normality) underlying statistical procedures will be performed and whether any corrective procedures will be applied (e.g., transformation or nonparametric tests).

< Analyses will be carried out as intention to treat. Analyses will be performed separately for each arm. Descriptive statistics will be reported for each variable and outcome. Means and standard deviations, or medians and interquartile ranges (IQR: 25th percentile to 75th percentile) will be reported for continuous variables, as appropriate. Frequencies and percentages will be reported for categorical variables. Unadjusted distribution of differences in liver steatosis and fibrosis, in ALT, in BMI relative to values at time of diagnosis will be reported. ANALYSIS OF THE PRIMARY EFFICACY ENDPOINT(S)

Title: < Role of probiotics in treatment of pediatric nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) patients by assessing with fibroscan >

Study Description: The goal of this study is to evaluate the role of probiotics in the treatment of pediatric NAFLD by evaluating for steatosis and fibrosis with a Fibroscan machine. This will be done by performing a fibroscan during each visit and comparing patients’ ALT at various intervals. This is an important study as current pediatric guidelines only recommend lifestyle modifications for the treatment of NAFLD and the use of ALT and sonogram to assess improvement as standard of care. We hypothesized that treatment with a probiotic will demonstrate an improvement in NAFLD as assessed by a fibroscan of liver which is good for the monitoring of steatosis and fibrosis. Additionally, analysis of fecal microbiome results may offer insight into targeted therapy in the future. <Protocol Title> Version <x.x>
